situation: Two blocks A (launch) and B (capture) communicate through an interconnect of known pipeline depth, and each block has its own internal budget. Need to write set_input_delay / set_output_delay at the boundary.
derivation: Start with the clock period T. Subtract the source register's Tco + clock-to-clock skew between A and B: T_launch_margin = T - Tco_A - skew. Subtract the capture register's setup requirement: T_capture_margin = T_launch_margin - Tsu_B. The remaining time is the budget for interconnect and any combinational logic in the boundary flop's input cone. A typical split: launch_clock_to_boundary_delay (max/min) = (T_capture_margin / 2) rounded toward the conservative side; the other half is implicitly absorbed by capture-side margin and skew. For output delay (B driving out): max_delay = T - Tco_B - Tsu_next_stage; min_delay = Tco_B - Thold_next_stage. The arithmetic shape: max_in_delay + min_in_delay spread should equal one clock period after subtracting Tco and Tsu.
wrong_way: Setting input_delay to 0.6T 'to be safe' and leaving the rest to the implementation tool. The tool then has no real budget for the interconnect and either under-builds retiming or, more commonly, pessimistically inflates the launch-side slack reporting while the capture side hides a real setup violation that surfaces only at gate-level signoff with extracted parasitics.
defense: Show the Tco/Tsu numbers from the cell library .lib, the skew from CTS reporting, and an explicit margin table: 'launch margin = T - Tco - skew; capture margin = launch - Tsu; interconnect gets the remainder.' Reviewers check the arithmetic sums to T.
signoff_risk: Too tight (budgeting interconnect only 5% of period when reality is 30%): setup violations appear at extracted signoff that were clean at synthesis; tapeout failure on hold is also possible if the min side was derived from the same pessimistic number. Too loose (giving interconnect 70% of period): the implementation tool builds slow paths in both blocks, area and timing closure slip, and the other block's owner has no real number to budget against — downstream re-budgeting cascade.

situation: A timing arc between two flops is functionally never exercised in one clock cycle — either it takes N cycles by design, or it never occurs at all. Must decide -false_path vs -multicycle_path with value N.
derivation: First, demand functional evidence: a waveform, a sequence diagram, or a protocol spec that proves the capture edge is N cycles after launch. If the data is valid N cycles later: set_multicycle_path N -setup -from launch -to capture, and also N-1 -hold -setup/-to_from swap so the hold check moves to the correct edge pair. The hold derivation: hold is checked one cycle before the active setup edge, so the hold multiplier must be N-1. If the path is genuinely never exercised: set_false_path, with a comment naming the functional reason. The arithmetic shape: with period T and MCP N, the setup budget becomes NT - Tco - Tsu; the hold check relaxes by (N-1)T.
wrong_way: Defaulting to set_false_path for anything that 'looks slow' to make timing clean. The tool removes it from optimization entirely, so the cells on that path never get sized for delay and never get checked for hold — at signoff the path either fails hold (if it is actually exercised under some test mode or scan) or draws excessive leakage because the cells were left at minimum size. The opposite wrong way: setting MCP N=2 when the real requirement is N=1, which doubles the setup budget and hides a real setup failure.
defense: Cite the protocol document, the sequence number in the spec, or a simulation waveform with the cycle count annotated. For false paths, name the functional state (e.g. 'config register write path, only asserted in test mode, covered by scan ATPG'). Reviewers ask: 'show me where this is exercised or prove it isn't.'
signoff_risk: False path when it should be MCP: the path is never optimized, shows no slack in reports, but if scan or a corner case exercises it, you have a hold or setup failure with no recovery path short of re-spinning metal. MCP when it should be false: a real functional race is hidden behind NT of slack and surfaces only in system validation as intermittent corruption.

situation: A signal crosses from clock domain A (freq fA) to domain B (freq fB) through a 2-flop synchronizer. The data is either a single bit, a pulse, or a multi-bit bus.
derivation: Constraining-wise, the path itself is set_false_path between the two clock domains — synchronizer reliability is structural, not timing. The actual engineering work is outside SDC: verify the synchronizer has no metastability MTBF below the budget, and that the data is held stable across the destination's sampling window. Derive the MTBF bound: MTBF = exp(t_res / C) / (fA * fB * fc) where t_res is the available resolution time and C, fc are technology constants; require MTBF >> product lifetime. Then derive the data-hold requirement: data must be stable for at least 2 periods of the faster clock plus the synchronizer latency. The SDC expression is just: set_false_path -from [get_clocks clkA] -to [get_clocks clkB] -through [get_pins sync*/D]. No arithmetic on the constraint itself; arithmetic is on the MTBF.
wrong_way: Setting a multicycle path between the domains to 'relax' the crossing — this implies the destination samples the source data predictably, which is the exact assumption a CDC breaks. The other wrong way: not constraining it at all and letting the tool attempt to close timing across the domain; the tool will invent impossible skew relationships and either fail to optimize or build paths that are formally closed but metastable in reality.
defense: Reference the synchronizer cell's MTBF report from the library, the CDC lint tool's structural check (no reconvergence, no glitch hazards on the control path), and the protocol requirement that data is stable for N destination cycles. Reviewers ask for the CDC lint log.
signoff_risk: If the false path is missing and the tool tries to time it: timing reports look clean but the silicon is unreliable. If the false path is applied where it shouldn't be (e.g. on a CDC genuinely requires a fixed relationship, like a source-synchronous interface misidentified as CDC): real functional failure. Either direction, the failure is in the field, not at signoff.

situation: Block A and block B are both being designed in parallel; neither has a placed netlist. Need a shared interface budget so both teams can implement independently and meet timing when integrated.
derivation: Negotiate a T_interface budget such that T_A_internal + T_B_internal + T_skew + T_interconnect <= T_period. Standard split: allocate 60% of T to the two blocks combined (30/30 or 40/20 depending on which is harder), 20% to interconnect, 20% to skew and margin. Write set_input_delay -max [0.3T] and -min [-0.1T] at B's boundary to constrain B's input paths, and the symmetric values at A's output. The min value is negative because B's launch clock can arrive after B's capture clock's reference edge — the derivation is: min_in_delay = -(T_co_A + interconnect_min - skew_max), which is often a small negative number.
wrong_way: Splitting 50/50 with no interconnect or skew margin because 'both teams said they need it all.' When integrated, every path fails by the interconnect delay that nobody reserved. The other wrong way: writing the budget based on the team's optimistic estimate of one block and giving the other block no slack to work with, causing one team to be unable to close regardless of effort.
defense: A spreadsheet with row per interface, columns for T_period, T_co, T_su, T_skew, T_interconnect, T_block_A, T_block_B, sum <= T. Each value sourced from prior silicon, library, or a documented estimate with a confidence column.
signoff_risk: Too tight (giving each block only 20% of T): neither team closes, schedule slip. Too loose (each block gets 45%, interconnect 10%): integration reveals interconnect is 30% not 10%, paths fail by 20% of T at extracted signoff — visible only after full-chip STA.

early over-constraining then relaxationu: RTL is stable but implementation hasn't started; need SDC so synthesis and initial floorplan can proceed. Real interconnect and skew are unknown.
derivation: Derive a pessimistic but defensible number: assume clock period T_real but constrain at T_pessimistic = T_real - delta, where delta covers the unknowns Typical delta = 10-15% of T, broken down as: 5% interconnect pessimism, 5% skew pessimism, 5% margin for unknown unknowns. Write the full SDC at. Track each delta in a header comment. As CTS, placement, and routing mature and the real numbers come in, subtract the consumed pessimism from delta and re-issue SDC at T_real - delta_remaining. The arithmetic: T_pessimistic = T_real * (1 - margin_sum), where margin_sum = sum of individually justified margins.
wrong_way: Constraining at T_real with no margin because 'we want the tool to optimize for the real target.' The tool reports clean timing on a synthesis netlist with no parasitics and no real skew, you sign off the SDC, and at placed-and-routed signoff every path fails by the interconnect and skew you never budgeted. The opposite: constraining so pessimistically that T_pessimistic < T_real - 30%; synthesis adds area and pipeline stages that have to be ripped out when the real SDC lands.
defense: A 'margin memo' attached to the SDC listing each pessimism source with its consumed amount the run that consumed it. Reviewers track the deltas shrinking as the design matures.
signoff_risk: If never relaxed: bloated area, unnecessary pipeline stages, hold fixing sprawl from over-aggressive CTS. If relaxed too early (before CTS exists): you lose the safety net and the post-CTS slack is negative. The schedule risk of a missed relaxation trigger is as bad as a missed tightening.

situation: An output drives an external device (DDR PHY, off-chip ASIC) that has its own clock, or an input is sampled by an external register on a board clock. The external clock is not in the FPGA/ASIC clock list.
derivation: Define a virtual clock with create_clock -name V_ext -period T_ext, where T_ext is the external device's clock period ( derived from a frequency mode and a PLL multiplier). Compute set_output_delay -max [T_ext - Tco_ext - Tsu_ext] and -min [-Tco_ext + Thold_ext] referenced to V_ext, at the FPGA/ASIC output pad. The arithmetic shape: max_delay represents the time from the external launch edge to the external capture edge minus the external setup; min_delay is the launch-to-capture window for hold. Inside the chip, the path from the internal flop to the pad must close against this external budget.
wrong_way: Using the internal clock for the output path and 'hoping' the external relationship works. The tool has no information about the external setup/hold and will produce paths that meet the internal period but violate the external device's timing. The other wrong way: declaring the virtual clock with the wrong period because the PLL mode was misread — every interface path is off by a fixed ratio.
defense: The external device datasheet with T_ext, Tco_ext, Tsu_ext, Thold_ext quoted. The PLL configuration register values showing the frequency mode. A timing diagram from the device vendor showing the relationship between V_ext and the data.
signoff_risk: Too tight (output_delay too large): the tool builds paths that can't close against the internal clock, area and timing closure slip. Too loose (output_delay too small): the silicon passes internal STA but fails the external device's setup/hold in the system — board bring-up shows intermittent data errors that look like signal integrity but are actually a wrong budget.

situation: A clock is generated internally by, PLL, or counter — it is not a primary input. It must be constrained so that all paths clocked by it are timed.
derivation: For a divided clock from a register: create_generated_clock -name clk_div -source [get_pins src_reg/CK] -divide_by N [get_pins div_reg/Q]. The SDC tool now knows clk_div has period N*T_src and infers the phase. For a PLL output: create_generated_clock -name clk_pll -source [get_pins pll/clkin] -multiply_by M -divide_by N [get_pins pll/clkout]. Then write set_false_path between the source clock and the generated clock domain, or set a multicycle if the relationship is known. The arithmetic: if generated clock frequency is f_src * M/N, the period is T_src * N/M, and any IO budget at the boundary uses T_generated.
wrong_way: Forgetting to constrain the generated clock — the tool sees it as unconstrained timing arcs and either errors out, treats all paths through it as false paths, or optimizes with garbage assumptions about the period. The other wrong way: using -multiply_by M without checking that the PLL is configured for that M in the actual silicon; the generated clock period in SDC doesn't match the silicon.
defense: The PLL configuration register settings, the divider ratio in the RTL, and a cross-check between the SDC value and the synthesized netlist's actual clock network. Reviewers confirm the source pin and the divide/multiply values match the design intent.
signoff_risk: Missing constraint: every path on the generated clock domain reports unconstrained or is dropped — silicon has unknown timing on those paths and likely fails in functional tests. Wrong divide ratio: the entire generated domain is timed against the wrong period; either over-constrained (area bloat) or under-constrained (setup failures at the rated frequency).

situation: A block has a port that is asynchronous to the system clock — e.g. a reset, a JTAG pin, an async memory interface, or a GPIO edge interrupt. The SDC must express 'do not time this' in a defensible way.
derivation: For an asynchronous reset: set_input_delay is not written; instead set_false_path -from [get_ports rst_n] (or set the reset as a non-timing port). For a JTAG TAP running on TCK which is unrelated to the system clock: create_clock on TCK, and_path between TCK and the system clock domains. For a GPIO that generates an interrupt on a chip-internal event: the path from the pad through the synchronizer to the interrupt controller is CDC and gets set_false_path with the synchronizer flops as -through. The arithmetic: no budget arithmetic; the engineering is structural (synchronizer chain) and the SDC just removes the path from timing closure.
wrong_way: Treating the async input as a normal synchronous input with set_input_delay derived from some guessed relationship. The tool will attempt to close timing against an impossible clock edge relationship and either fail outright or, worse, succeed formally because of the false assumption and fail metastably in silicon. The other wrong way: setting set_false_path on the entire async port including any synchronizer flops, removing the synchronizer itself from timing — now there's no timing check on the synchronizer's internal setup/hold either.
defense: For resets: cite the architecture spec that the reset is asynchronously asserted and synchronously deasserted, and name the sync flops. For JTAG: cite IEEE 1149.1 and show TCK is independent. For GPIO interrupts: show the synchronizer cell and the CDC lint pass.
signoff_risk: If the path is timed when it shouldn't be: tool optimizes for a non-existent timing relationship, silicon has metastability-induced failures. If the false path is too broad and covers legitimate synchronous logic: that logic never gets optimized, area and timing on real paths suffer, hold failures on scan or functional paths hidden by the false path.

situation: Data and clock travel together from an external device (typically a DRAM or serializer) into the chip on matched-length board traces. The clock is forwarded with the data, so the source-synchronous capture is in the data-eye of the forwarded clock.
derivation: Define a virtual clock for the forwarded clock at the source's frequency. Compute the data valid window at the chip's input pad: T_bit = 1/f_data. The data eye at the pad is T_bit - Tco_skew - ISI, where Tco_skew is the source's clock-to-output variation across lanes/bits and ISI is inter-symbol interference from the channel. Then set_input_delay -max = T_co_max + flight_time_max, -min = T_co_min + flight_time_min, both referenced to the forwarded-clock virtual clock. The internal capture path must close against max - min. Arithmetic shape: max_in_delay - min_in_delay <= T_bit - setup_margin - hold_margin; this is the effective data eye width the internal path must fit in.
wrong_way: Treating the forwarded clock as if it were asynchronous to the data and writing a CDC-style constraint. The data is not metastable — it's launched by the same forwarded clock and the relationship is fixed for the duration of a burst. The [blocked]
